analysis.one_liner: Narrows the "joint employer" rule, shielding franchisors and subcontractors from liability for wage and labor violations.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a vote after being referred to the House Education and Labor Committee on the day it was introduced, with all 69 sponsors and cosponsors Republicans.
analysis.plain_summary: Under federal labor law, two companies can sometimes be treated as "joint employers" of the same workers — for example, a fast-food corporation and its local franchise owner, or a factory and the temp agency that staffs it. When that happens, the big company can be held responsible if workers are underpaid or fired illegally, and unions can bargain with the corporation that actually calls the shots. This bill rewrites the National Labor Relations Act and the Fair Labor Standards Act so a company counts as a joint employer only if it directly and immediately controls essential work conditions like hiring, firing, pay, schedules, and discipline [S2] [S3]. That narrow test would let brand-name franchisors, staffing agencies, and companies using contractors keep their distance when workers at the bottom are shortchanged [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Large franchisors (fast-food chains, hotels, convenience stores) and companies that use staffing agencies and contractors. If a brand or parent company only sets rules, royalties, and standards but doesn't directly hire, fire, or supervise workers day to day, it could no longer be held liable when a franchisee or agency commits wage violations or unlawful firings, and it would no longer have to bargain with unions representing franchise or subcontracted workers. Franchise owners also gain, since they would bear the liability alone even when the franchisor dictates prices and operating terms.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Franchisors, staffing agencies, and outsourcing companies

how_it_helps.text: Amends the National Labor Relations Act so a company is a joint employer only if it 'directly, actually, and immediately' exercises significant control over hiring, firing, pay, benefits, day-to-day supervision, schedules, and discipline.

Applies the same narrow standard to the Fair Labor Standards Act, the law behind federal minimum-wage and overtime claims, shrinking the pool of companies that can be sued or fined when franchise or subcontracted workers are underpaid.
Franchise owners benefit from not sharing liability with the brand they buy into, though they also lose the argument that corporate rules forced their hand.

analysis.who_pays: Workers at franchises, temp-agency placements, and subcontracted workplaces. They would lose the ability to hold the powerful company at the top responsible for wage theft, overtime violations, and retaliation, and unions would lose the ability to bargain directly with the corporation that controls the terms — leaving small franchisees and agencies as the only parties with the money and the obligation, and workers at the mercy of whoever directly signs their checks.
analysis.who_pays_short: Franchise and subcontracted workers, and unions

drawbacks.text: The bill removes the main legal tool that holds large brands responsible for wage and hour violations committed against workers who wear the brand's uniform but are technically employed by a franchisee or staffing agency, pushing labor-law enforcement down onto small, thinly capitalized employers.

It would weaken unions' ability to bargain with the corporation that actually sets franchise prices, technology, and operating standards, since a brand that avoids 'direct and immediate' control could no longer be treated as an employer.

A good-faith objection: the broad joint-employer standard did risk making franchisors legally responsible for employment decisions they don't actually make, which some small franchise owners said exposed them to liability and made brands reluctant to invest in franchise networks — this bill was designed to draw a clean line at actual day-to-day control.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill gives franchise chains, staffing firms, and outsourcing companies a clear liability shield and relieves franchisors of legal responsibility for conditions in their networks, but the cost falls on the millions of workers who would lose recourse to the deep-pocketed company that actually sets the terms of their jobs, and on unions trying to bargain with those companies. The trade runs almost entirely from workers toward concentrated corporate interests.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. James Comer (R-KY) introduced the bill on May 13, 2021, with 68 Republican cosponsors and no Democratic support.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor on the same day, which was the only action it ever received.
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — appears in the bill's complete action history before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
The committee's Democratic majority never advanced the bill, so the broader joint-employer standards it sought to rewrite remained in place.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the existing broader joint-employer standards stayed in place, so franchise and subcontracted workers and unions kept their ability to reach the large corporations that shape their jobs. The companies the bill would have shielded — big franchisors and staffing agencies — are no worse off than before, but they did not get the rollback they sought; the safest bet for them is that the bill's sponsor, now chairing a committee in the next Congress, could revive the same language.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Franchise and subcontracted workers kept protections

for.name: International Franchise Association
for.what_they_did: Endorsed the Save Local Business Act and lobbied for a narrow joint-employer standard.

against.name: House Education and Labor Committee majority
against.role: Committee controlling whether the bill got a hearing or vote
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to committee and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 69 sponsors and cosponsors were House Republicans, and the Democratic-controlled committee that received the bill never acted on it, so support was entirely one-party.

industries.note: The bill would shield brand-name franchisors from being treated as joint employers of franchise workers, meaning wage theft or illegal firings at a franchise could no longer reach the corporation — even when the corporation dictates prices, technology, and operating standards. Workers wearing the brand's name would lose their main path to the deep-pocketed company behind it.

Companies that supply and supervise temporary and outsized workers would only be liable when they directly control essential employment terms, reducing exposure under the minimum-wage and overtime law for misclassification and unpaid hours.

Local franchise owners would no longer share liability with the brand, but they would also lose the counterweight of a big company being on the hook when corporate rules squeeze workers — the liability simply lands on them.

Under the National Labor Relations Act, a narrow joint-employer test makes it far harder to bargain with a franchisor or parent company that sets the real terms of work, weakening union organizing in franchised and subcontracted workplaces.
